claims.text: In healthy volunteers, a single 25 mg dose left enduring functional brain changes “largely absent” one month later, though some diffusion-imaging and network-modularity signals persisted; what lasted was mainly psychological: well-being and insight.
claims.basis: Lyons: within-subjects, 28 enrolled, exploratory, not pre-registered. “Largely absent” is the authors' phrasing.
claims.wouldChangeIf: A pre-registered, adequately powered study in healthy volunteers finds enduring functional brain change at one month or later. That would move this from preliminary to active debate; an independent replication of the null would move it toward established.

claims.text: In depression patients given two doses with psychological support, psilocybin increased global brain integration (lower network modularity), and the size of that change tracked the antidepressant response.
claims.basis: Daws: two trials; correlational; subscription article (facts cited, figures not reused).
claims.wouldChangeIf: An independent research program fails to find increased global integration in depression patients, or finds it without any link to antidepressant response. A second independent replication would move this toward established.

claims.text: Those integration changes were seen up to three weeks after the second of two doses; the study did not establish how much longer they last.
claims.basis: Daws: fMRI at baseline and ~3 weeks post-dose; longer-term durability not measured.

claims.text: In mice, one dose drives activity-dependent structural rewiring: dendritic-spine remodeling in frontal cortex that strengthens some routes and weakens recurrent cortical loops, and that depends on the drug-evoked neural activity itself.
claims.basis: Jiang: C57BL/6 mice, rabies-tracing; silencing a presynaptic region during dosing disrupts the rewiring, evidence it is activity-dependent.
claims.wouldChangeIf: An independent lab fails to replicate activity-dependent spine remodeling, or shows the rewiring survives silencing of presynaptic input. Either would move the mechanism from preliminary to active debate.

claims.text: In mice, psychedelics reopen a “critical period” for social-reward learning, and the window's length is proportional to each drug's acute subjective duration: roughly two weeks for psilocybin, up to four for ibogaine.
claims.basis: Nardou/Dölen: shared across psychedelics; mechanism via oxytocin-mediated LTD and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Durations are the paper's mouse findings.

claims.text: The popular “psilocybin opens a four-week window that rewires your brain” collapses different things: it appears to borrow ibogaine's four-week mouse figure (psilocybin's was ~2 weeks) or to stretch a one-month mouse spine result, and it merges a behavior-specific mouse finding with human brain imaging, none of which is the same claim.
claims.basis: The mouse critical-period result is about social-reward learning, not general brain rewiring; the four-week figure is ibogaine's, not psilocybin's; human durable functional change is modest at best (Lyons).

claims.text: In seven healthy adults scanned repeatedly before, during and after a 25 mg dose, psilocybin acutely desynchronized brain networks far more than an active control (methylphenidate). Most changes faded, but weaker coupling between the anterior hippocampus and the default-mode network persisted for weeks.
claims.basis: Siegel: precision functional mapping (many repeated scans of a few people rather than one scan of many); n = 7; the only study here with a psychoactive control. Washington University group; Carhart-Harris is one co-author of 33, so it counts as a separate program tied to the Imperial one. Participants were scanned for three weeks after the dose; at an open-label revisit 6 to 12 months later the coupling was back at baseline, though that sample (n = 4) was not powered for small changes.

claims.text: In the largest trial here (233 people with treatment-resistant depression), a single 25 mg dose reduced depression scores more than a 1 mg control at three weeks; 10 mg did not separate from control, and a lasting benefit beyond three weeks was not established.
claims.basis: Goodwin: phase 2b, randomized, double-blind, three doses (25, 10, 1 mg) with psychological support, after participants stopped their antidepressants; primary outcome MADRS change at week 3. Sponsor-funded (COMPASS Pathways). Adverse events, including suicidal ideation or self-injury, occurred in every dose group. A clinical outcome, not brain imaging.

claims.text: In a six-week double-blind trial of 59 people with moderate-to-severe depression, two 25 mg doses of psilocybin did not significantly beat daily escitalopram on the primary depression score; secondary measures leaned toward psilocybin but were not corrected for multiple comparisons.
claims.basis: Carhart-Harris 2021: phase 2, active comparator (escitalopram plus 1 mg psilocybin); primary outcome QIDS-SR-16 at week 6, which may be short for escitalopram to reach full effect. A clinical outcome, not imaging. Included because part of Daws's imaging comes from this trial's patients.

claims.text: In mice, a single dose increased the density and size of dendritic spines in frontal cortex within a day, and the higher spine density was still measurable about a month later.
claims.basis: Shao: chronic two-photon imaging of the same dendrites in living mice before and after one dose. Kwan lab: the same lab as Jiang 2026, so the two mouse rewiring papers are one program.

claims.text: Five of the human studies here come from one research program (Carhart-Harris and colleagues), so they are not independent replications; two other human findings (Siegel, Goodwin) each list him as one co-author among many.
claims.basis: Lyons, Daws and the 2021 escitalopram trial share a lead or senior author (Carhart-Harris) and several co-authors (Erritzoe, Nutt, and others), and part of Daws's imaging comes from that trial's patients. Pasquini re-analyses the Lyons sample, and Harding re-analyses the escitalopram trial; both list Carhart-Harris and Nutt. The five papers rest on three samples (the Lyons volunteers, the escitalopram trial, and Daws's open-label trial). Siegel (33 authors) and Goodwin (74 authors) each list Carhart-Harris mid-list. Verifiable authorship and data facts. (Version 2.2 changed “Three” to “Five” when Pasquini and Harding were added.)

claims.text: A large multimodal human study (PsiConnect, 62 participants, follow-up to one year) is mapping psilocybin's effects across imaging methods, but it is a preprint, and not yet a settled result.
claims.basis: bioRxiv preprint (not peer-reviewed), CC-BY-NC-ND; a dataset/methods contribution rather than a specific finding.

claims.text: In 15 healthy adults, one dose did not significantly increase synaptic density one week later overall, measured by SV2A PET in frontal cortex and hippocampus. In an exploratory comparison, participants dosed in a therapy-like room showed a greater frontal increase than those dosed in an MRI scanner; the hippocampal difference was smaller, with an interval that included zero.
claims.basis: Johansen: [11C]UCB-J PET at baseline and one week after 0.3 mg/kg psilocybin, in an open-label, single-arm study with no placebo. The VT analysis, run at an interim look on the 12 participants with complete arterial blood data, found no significant increase (mean change: frontal cortex 0.3 mL/cm3, SD 2.6; hippocampus 0.3 mL/cm3, SD 2.0; one-sided p = 0.29 and 0.33), and the study was stopped for futility; BPND, computed for all 15, showed no significant increase either (mean change: frontal cortex −0.01, SD 0.35; hippocampus 0.01, SD 0.28). Setting difference in the change in VT: frontal cortex 3.0 mL/cm3 (95% CI 0.4 to 5.5), hippocampus 1.9 mL/cm3 (95% CI −0.3 to 3.9); the authors call it preliminary and hypothesis-generating. With no placebo arm, the authors note they may have underestimated an increase, because other SV2A studies saw drops at a second scan. The room group's own change in VT: frontal cortex 1.1 mL/cm3 (95% CI −0.5 to 2.7), hippocampus 0.8 mL/cm3 (95% CI −0.5 to 2.1). The Methods list participants 1 to 5 as dosed in the scanner and 6 to 15 in the room; the main text does not say how setting was allocated. SV2A density is a marker of synaptic density in living people, not a count of dendritic spines.
claims.wouldChangeIf: A larger or independently replicated PET study finding a significant overall increase in synaptic density after one dose would move the human question to active debate. A preregistered test of the setting effect would show whether the subgroup difference holds.

claims.text: Re-analysing the same healthy volunteers as Lyons, a study that also used computational modelling found activity in fronto-striatal-thalamic circuits more dynamic four weeks after 25 mg than four weeks after the 1 mg control dose, but only a trend against the pre-dose baseline; the authors call the evidence weak to moderate.
claims.basis: Pasquini: secondary analysis of the Lyons trial's resting fMRI, 25 psychedelic-naive adults in a fixed order (1 mg, then 25 mg four weeks later; no placebo, no randomized order). Dynamic functional homogeneity across 28 fronto-striatal-thalamic regions was lower four weeks after 25 mg than four weeks after 1 mg (t(24) = 2.87, p = 0.008) and trended lower than baseline (t(24) = 1.92, p = 0.06); the paper reads lower homogeneity as more dynamic, more variable activity across a scan, and its Methods say FDR correction “was used to adjust p-values, unless specified otherwise”, without saying which applies to these t-tests. Whole-brain homogeneity fell at both later scans, which the authors attribute to order effects. The modelled drop in structure-function coupling was stable across repeated simulations, which the authors say “do not represent independent biological samples”; its group-level permutation test was a trend (p = 0.064). The effective-connectivity results rest only on stability statistics across simulations. Same sample and program as Lyons (Lyons and Carhart-Harris are co-authors), so not independent. Full text read; CC BY-NC 4.0, cited only.

claims.text: In ten healthy volunteers given low-to-moderate doses (5 to 20 mg; a preprint), brain connectivity one week after a dose showed one dose-dependent increase within a network that survived correction, and none of the 77 dose-dependent changes in single connections did; how strongly the dose altered conscious state was linked to wider connectivity changes, many surviving correction at the network level.
claims.basis: Bhagavan: medRxiv preprint, not peer reviewed. Ten healthy volunteers each received three doses between 5 and 20 mg in randomized, blinded order at least a week apart; resting fMRI at baseline and one week after a single dose (registered ACTRN12621000560897). Per the abstract: 77 dose-dependent edge changes (76 increases, 1 decrease, of 1275) with none surviving correction; one dose-dependent between-network increase (of 21) and one within-network increase (of 7), the latter surviving correction; changes in conscious state were associated with connectivity change, many surviving correction. Abstract only: the full text was unreachable, so the network involved and effect sizes are not checked.

claims.text: In small open-label studies of chronic cluster headache, patients given three doses of 0.14 mg/kg a week apart showed no statistically significant average change in brain microstructure one week after the last dose (11 patients), while in 10 patients a change in hypothalamic connectivity tracked how much their attacks fell.
claims.basis: Madsen 2024: 10 patients, 0.14 mg/kg in weeks five, six and seven, fMRI the day before the first dose and one week after the last; attacks fell 31% on average (SD 31), and the change in hypothalamic-diencephalic connectivity correlated with the change in attack frequency (R = -0.81, pFWER = 0.03). Brendstrup-Brix 2026: 11 patients on the same schedule (EPOCH trial, NCT04280055), diffusion MRI before and one week after; psilocybin “was not associated with statistically significant changes in brain microstructure or water diffusivity”, though most patients showed lower white-matter diffusivity and neurite volume. Abstracts only (full texts unreachable); whether the two samples overlap is not checked. No placebo. One Copenhagen program, the same as Johansen 2026 (Knudsen and Madsen are authors on all three).

claims.text: In depression patients from the escitalopram trial, task fMRI three weeks after the second psilocybin session showed less surprise-related activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and angular gyrus than in patients on escitalopram, and, within the psilocybin group, more activity in sensory regions, which did not differ significantly from escitalopram.
claims.basis: Harding: secondary analysis of the phase II psilocybin versus escitalopram trial (NCT03429075), 22 psilocybin and 19 escitalopram patients with usable fMRI, scanned the day before the first dose and six weeks later, three weeks after the second psilocybin session. Ventromedial prefrontal treatment-by-time interaction F(1,39) = 7.074, p = 0.0113; the within-group decrease after psilocybin t(21) = 2.195, p = 0.0395, with no correction across the three regions of interest described. No significant change in the nucleus accumbens or superior temporal gyrus, and no significant correlation between these regions and anhedonia or music ratings; whole-brain maps cluster-corrected; baseline vmPFC differed between groups at trend level (p = 0.081). Surprise-related affective ratings showed no significant change after psilocybin (they fell after escitalopram). A published correction changed the abstract to “decreased activation in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex”; this claim follows the correction. One song, one task. Same trial and program as Carhart-Harris 2021 and part of Daws 2022. Full text read; CC BY 4.0, cited only.

claims.text: Two 2026 systematic reviews flag limits in human follow-up imaging: one found follow-up scans lacking in most psilocybin fMRI studies, with lasting effects reported up to four weeks; the other, in depression, grouped some network changes as “Longer-term changes (5+ weeks)” without saying in its abstract whether that is when scans were taken, and warned that many studies reuse overlapping datasets.
claims.basis: Farré-Colomés (full text read): 36 articles from 20 datasets, published between February 2012 and July 2024; “follow-up scanning timepoints were lacking in most of the studies”, and studies with follow-up scans suggest effects “lasting up to 4 weeks after intake”; PRISMA, not preregistered, no named risk-of-bias tool. Sabbah (abstract only, full text unreachable): 11 studies in depression, PROSPERO-registered; early (0 to 4 weeks) changes included lower modularity and higher integration, and “Longer-term changes (5+ weeks)” included higher prefronto-parietal and salience-network connectivity; “Many studies reused overlapping datasets with high exploratory flexibility and risk of bias.” Which studies carry the 5+ week finding is not checked. Farré-Colomés, covering depression studies to July 2024, says none “incorporated follow-up fMRI scans” and that a vmPFC-IPC increase “predicted treatment response at 5 weeks”, so Sabbah's 5+ weeks may be outcome timing rather than scan timing. Two separate teams.

claims.text: In rats, a single dose of psilocybin or of the 5-HT2A agonist 25CN-NBOH reduced immobility in a forced swim test for at least three months; several months after treatment, prefrontal layer 5 neurons still showed changed resting potential, firing and synaptic excitation, while synaptic density and spine types in treated rats did not differ from controls.
claims.basis: Kramer (Nichols lab): per the abstract, there were “no overt behavioral differences between psilocybin and 25CN-NBOH treated animals” and functional plasticity “was evident for both psychedelics”; the microscopy and gene-expression nulls compare “control and psychedelic-treated” animals, and the abstract does not say whether psilocybin was tested on its own for them. Brain-slice electrophysiology found functional plasticity “several months after treatment”; microscopy of the recorded neurons found no differences in synaptic density or spine classification, and gene expression for several synaptic markers did not differ. Abstract only: the full text was unreachable, so sample sizes, exact timepoints and effect sizes are not checked. The longest-lasting change after a single dose reported in this synthesis, from a lab separate from the mouse spine studies.

claims.text: In rats, one week after a single dose, psilocybin on its own changed relative brain glucose uptake in few measures: uptake rose in the insula and the across-rat correlation between prefrontal and insula uptake strengthened, and no whole-brain cluster survived correction for psilocybin alone; the paper's headline one-week hypometabolism pools psilocybin with LSD and 2C-B.
claims.basis: Gudmundsen: 12 Long Evans rats of both sexes per drug group (11 analysed for LSD), [18F]FDG-PET at baseline, acutely and one week after 1 mg/kg psilocybin given under the skin, each group compared with its own baseline (no drug-versus-saline contrast described; the saline cohort showed no change between repeated scans). Uptake is normalized to the whole-brain mean, so it is relative. Insula mean change in normalized uptake 0.16 (adjusted p < 0.05); prefrontal-insula covariance (a correlation across rats, not a within-brain connection) change ΔZ = 1.53 (adjusted p = 0.04); thalamus-prefrontal change not significant after correction (adjusted p = 0.61). “Psilocybin produced no acute or persistent clusters surviving FDR correction.” The paper's Results (“despite not reaching significance in individual drug contrasts”) and Discussion (“significantly reduced for psilocybin”) disagree about psilocybin's own change in the pooled one-week clusters. Full text read; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, cited only.

claims.text: In diet-induced obese male mice given one dose, synaptic protein puncta counts (PSD-95, synapsin-1) in prefrontal cortex and hypothalamus did not differ from controls 30 days later.
claims.basis: Keenan: male C57BL/6J mice made obese on a high-fat diet, one 1 mg/kg intraperitoneal dose, then either kept on the high-fat diet or switched to low-fat chow; brains taken 30 days later; 5 to 6 mice per group, between groups rather than repeated imaging. “Psilocybin had no influence on positive puncta of synapsin-1, PSD-95 or co-localisation of both proteins (i.e., synapses)” in the three regions. The authors note that spine density peaks around day 7, so by day 30 a difference “may not have been substantial enough to be detected with the methods used here”. Puncta counts are not spine counts. Full text read; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, cited only.

claims.text: In two studies, repeated dosing in adolescent rodents was followed by brain differences weeks to months later whose meaning is unclear: mice dosed five times in adolescence showed smaller regional brain volumes, altered diffusion and higher connectivity on MRI as adults, and rats dosed daily for a week showed a hippocampal neurogenesis marker (NeuroD1) that paralleled antidepressant-like behaviour, measured 16 days after treatment.
claims.basis: Sahoo (full text read): 28 mice, an approximate dose of 3.0 mg/kg by gavage every other day on postnatal days 40 to 50; MRI from day 85 to day 176. Normalized regional volumes fell in both sexes (males p < 0.001, females p < 0.05) and pooled diffusion measures rose (p < 0.0001); no area-level sex-by-treatment effect survived FDR correction, no standardized effect sizes are given, the regional tests state no correction and appear to pair brain areas rather than animals, the resting-state sample (10 versus 11) pooled the sexes, and the paper's timeline is internally inconsistent. Funded by Ekam Imaging, in which two authors hold a partnership interest. García-Cabrerizo (abstract only): adolescent Sprague-Dawley rats of both sexes, 0.3 or 1 mg/kg by mouth daily for 7 days; hippocampal neurogenesis markers measured 1 and 16 days after treatment, with NeuroD1 paralleling antidepressant-like effects seen up to 15 days. Repeated dosing in development, not one adult dose; two separate labs.

relations.label: population difference
relations.statement: The headline conflict (“it rewires the brain” vs “changes are largely absent”) partly tracks who was dosed: broad network change lasting weeks has been reported in patients; in healthy volunteers, lasting change has been narrower (Siegel) or largely absent (Lyons). Dose count, psychological support and timing differ too.
relations.basis: Two different populations and analyses; the field genuinely debates whether durable change is population-specific or a general drug effect.

relations.label: measures differently
relations.statement: The studies also split by what they measure: structural markers (spines, white-matter) can persist while functional day-to-day activity resets, though here the clearest structural persistence is in mice, so this split overlaps species. “Rewiring” and “function returned to baseline” can both be true.
relations.basis: Structural vs functional measures answer different questions on different timescales.

relations.label: mechanism for
relations.statement: The mouse rewiring is one candidate mechanism for the human network changes, but that is a cross-species inference, not a demonstration in humans.
relations.basis: Mechanism shown in mice by one lab (Jiang, Shao); human evidence is imaging-level and correlational. Nardou's oxytocin-dependent critical-period mechanism is a rival candidate.

relations.label: measures differently
relations.statement: Partly in tension, same population: a dense-scanning study of seven healthy adults found one functional change (weaker hippocampus–default-mode coupling) lasting weeks, where the group study found enduring functional change “largely absent” at a month. Different designs and timepoints; together they are consistent with narrow lasting change, or with changes that fade between a few weeks and a month.
relations.basis: Siegel (n = 7, many scans each, weeks) and Lyons (28 enrolled, group analysis, one month) ask the same question with different instruments. Separate programs, tied by one shared co-author (Carhart-Harris).

relations.label: extends
relations.statement: A larger, sponsor-funded, single-dose trial from a separate program (one shared co-author) reports patient effects at the same three-week mark and did not establish a lasting benefit beyond it; Daws's imaging stops at three weeks. The shared horizon is partly by design.
relations.basis: Goodwin measures symptoms and followed patients past week 3; Daws measures brain networks and did not image beyond three weeks. Agreement on timescale, not on mechanism.

relations.label: measures differently
relations.statement: Same patients, two measures: part of Daws's integration finding comes from a trial where psilocybin did not clearly beat escitalopram on its primary depression score. The integration signal is evidence about the brain, not proof of a better treatment.
relations.basis: Daws analyzed imaging from two trials, one of them Carhart-Harris 2021. One program, so this is context, not independent support.

relations.label: extends
relations.statement: Jiang's network-scale rewiring builds on the same lab's finding that the new spines persist for a month: one lab refining its own result, not an independent replication.
relations.basis: Shao and Jiang share the senior author (Kwan) and several co-authors.

relations.label: measures differently
relations.statement: The most direct human test of the synapse-growth idea so far found no significant overall increase in synaptic density one week after a dose, while mice show more and larger dendritic spines within a day that last a month. Different species, measures and timepoints, and the human study is small; an exploratory setting comparison points the other way in the frontal cortex.
relations.basis: Johansen (human SV2A PET, n = 15, one week) against Shao (mouse two-photon spine imaging, one month). SV2A PET and spine counts are different measures of synapses.

relations.label: measures differently
relations.statement: Same healthy-volunteer sample (25 in the re-analysis; Lyons enrolled 28), a different analysis: where the primary report found enduring functional change “largely absent” at one month, a re-analysis finds activity in fronto-striatal-thalamic circuits more dynamic four weeks after 25 mg than four weeks after 1 mg, only a trend against baseline, and calls the evidence weak to moderate. One program re-reading its own data, not a replication.
relations.basis: Pasquini reuses the Lyons sample and fMRI; Lyons and Carhart-Harris are authors on both.

relations.label: measures differently
relations.statement: Different species, timepoint and method: in mice, more spines a month after one dose; in rats given psilocybin or 25CN-NBOH, several months after one dose, changed neuron function with no difference in synaptic density or spine types (the abstract does not say whether the structural result holds for psilocybin alone). The rat study's authors read this as “enduring function plasticity rather than structural plasticity”; neither study measured at the other's timepoint.
relations.basis: Kramer (rats, slice electrophysiology and microscopy, months; abstract only) against Shao (mice, two-photon imaging, one month). Separate labs. The structural null is reported for “psychedelic-treated” rats; the abstract does not separate the two drugs.

relations.label: measures differently
relations.statement: Around the one-month mark, two-photon imaging found higher spine density in healthy mice, while synaptic protein puncta counts in obese mice found no difference. Different measures, populations and labs, and the second study's authors say that, because spine density peaks around day 7, by day 30 a difference may have been too small for their methods to detect.
relations.basis: Keenan (obese male mice, PSD-95 and synapsin-1 puncta, 30 days, 5 to 6 mice per group, between groups) against Shao (mice, repeated spine imaging of the same dendrites, about a month). Puncta counts are not spine counts.

relations.label: measures differently
relations.statement: Same trial, a different task: alongside the resting-state integration finding, task fMRI in the escitalopram trial's patients shows changed brain responses to musical surprise three weeks after the second session; unlike the integration finding, these did not track symptoms. It adds a measure at the same three-week horizon, not an independent confirmation or a longer follow-up.
relations.basis: Harding and part of Daws come from the same trial (NCT03429075) and program; in that trial both scanned three weeks after the second psilocybin session (Daws also used an open-label trial). Harding found no significant correlation between these regions and anhedonia or music ratings.

relations.label: population difference
relations.statement: Read across the nine studies in version 2.0, the “does it rewire the brain?” conflict may largely be explained by three axes: population (global network change in patients, imaged up to three weeks after the second of two doses; in healthy volunteers after one dose, so far only narrower lasting changes, such as weaker hippocampus–default-mode coupling for weeks), measure (lasting structural change is shown mainly in mice, so this axis overlaps species; in humans, some functional changes last weeks while most reset), and species (mechanism is clearest in mice). Two questions this raises for the field: is the broad human signal a psilocybin-specific response of the depressed brain rather than a general effect of the drug? And since three of the five human findings come from one research program and the other two share a co-author with it, how much is independent replication versus one network refining its own result? (Caveats that could also explain the split: population is confounded with dose, psychological support and timing (patients had two doses with support and were scanned at up to three weeks, healthy volunteers one dose at one month) and the one healthy-volunteer study scanning at weeks, Siegel, did find a lasting change; every human imaging sample here is small; brain integration may follow mood improvement rather than drive it; and in patients, neither brain nor symptom effects are established beyond about three weeks.) Johansen 2026, added in version 2.1, found no significant overall increase in human synaptic density one week after a dose; this reading has not yet been re-tested against it, nor against the twelve studies added in version 2.2.
relations.basis: PsychDoc's cross-source reading, offered to the field as a question, not asserted as fact.
